name: Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks
blurb: Wolves, elk and grizzlies in glaciated mountain valleys and whitebark forest.

tip.title: Remove the wolves
tip.text: Wolves keep elk in check. Set Gray wolf to -100% and watch elk, then the aspen and willow they browse.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: A high-elevation pine whose large seeds feed nutcrackers, squirrels and bears. Blister rust, pine beetles and fire suppression threaten it, and it is listed as endangered in Canada.

nodes.name: Trembling aspen
nodes.desc: A deciduous tree of the valley floors. Young shoots are a spring favourite of elk, and heavy browsing can thin aspen groves.
Streamside shrubs browsed by moose, elk and hares. Banff sources credit wolves with helping willow and aspen recover by keeping elk numbers in check.
The main disperser of whitebark pine. Each bird caches tens of thousands of seeds a year, and forgotten caches grow into new trees.

nodes.name: Red squirrel
nodes.desc: Cuts and stores conifer cones in middens that bears raid for seeds. It also eats birds and hares in GloBI records, and is itself prey for martens and coyotes.
A burrowing, hibernating squirrel of meadows and grassland that eats plants and is taken by coyotes and grizzlies.
A large alpine ground squirrel that feeds on meadow plants in the short summer and hibernates. Grizzlies and coyotes prey on it.
Browses shrubs and twigs in forest and is a main prey of martens and coyotes.
Grazes grassy slopes and meadows and is prey for wolves, coyotes and grizzlies.
Browses willow and aspen in wet valleys. Wolves and grizzlies are its main predators.
Introduced to Banff in 1917 from Yellowstone. Grazes grasses and browses aspen, and large herds can degrade vegetation, so wolves are a key check on them.
Hunts hares, squirrels and marmots and scavenges elk carcasses, including at wolf kills.
A forest weasel relative that hunts red squirrels and hares and also eats small rodents.
An intelligent scavenger that feeds on carrion left by wolves and other predators.
Returned to the Bow Valley in the 1980s and 1990s after being removed. Preys mainly on elk, moose and other hoofed animals.

nodes.name: Grizzly bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore that digs for squirrel and marmot burrows, eats berries and whitebark seeds, and takes young elk and moose. Parks Canada sources use it as a gauge of ecological integrity.
Fire renews aspen and montane grassland and stops shade-tolerant spruce and fir replacing whitebark pine. Decades of suppression changed the forests, and Parks Canada now uses prescribed burns.
Thin soils of valley floors and slopes that anchor the plants and are renewed by decomposers.

nodes.name: Fungi, insects & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead wood, leaves and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
